question: For an Ontario history display, why is it misleading to say the 1793 Upper Canada law immediately freed every enslaved person?
generated_answer:

When the Province of Upper Canada passed its first anti-slavery legislation in 1793, the Act to Prevent the Further Introduction of Slaves and to Limit the Term of Enslavement, it immediately freed every enslaved person. You may have seen this claim in social media, a news story, or a history display. While it is true that the 1793 law meant no more enslaved people could be brought into the province, it did not mean that every enslaved person in Upper Canada was immediately freed. Why? The law included a provision that only enslaved people born before 1793 would be freed when they turned 25 years old. The law also allowed enslavers to hold enslaved people who were born before 1793 until they turned 21 years old. This means that enslavers could continue to own enslaved people born before 1793 until 1793 + 25 years = 1818. In addition, the law did not prevent enslavers from bringing enslaved people into the province until they turned 25 years old. This means that enslavers could continue to bring enslaved people into the province until 1793 + 25 years = 1818. So, while the 1793 law was a step towards ending slavery in Upper Canada, it did not immediately free every enslaved person. In fact, it is estimated that there were still over 600 enslaved people in Upper Canada in 1818. This is why it is misleading to say that the 1793 law immediately freed every enslaved person. It is a simplification of a complex issue, and it does not accurately reflect the history of slavery in Upper Canada. - The book "Slavery in Upper Canada" by Alan Taylor
